paras: The attempted lynching of Samuel Johnson took place near Helena, Georgia, on Tuesday night, August 4, 1903, when a mob hanged Johnson, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, and left him for dead. Black passersby cut him down and revived him, and he was later found near Macon and jailed. Northern papers ran it under headlines such as "Lynched Negro Still Alive."
The woman Johnson was accused of assaulting near Helena is not named in the coverage.

The mob hanged Johnson from a tree on Tuesday night and, by his own account, left immediately after "swinging him to a limb." Soon afterward a party of Black men found the body and cut it down. Johnson appeared dead but revived once the rope was removed.

His rescuers brought him to the outskirts of Macon and hid him in a hut. On August 7 health officers, told that a man there was sick, found him. The rope had cut deeply into his neck, and dispatches described him as "in a dangerous condition" or "in a dying condition."

Johnson was removed to the jail, and the Tribune's correspondent reported that if he recovered he would be "returned to the scene of his crime." A brief printed on August 12 said he was still in jail. No report of arrests, a trial, or his later fate was found.

Macon dispatches dated August 7 and 8 ran on August 8 in the New-York Tribune and the Waterbury Evening Democrat. The Tribune headlined its telegraphed account "LYNCHED NEGRO STILL ALIVE" and added the subhead "Mob Will Have Another Chance," though its text called Johnson only "accused" of the assault. The Waterbury paper's "Lynched Negro Still Lives" went further, calling him "the negro who attacked a white woman" and treating the charge as settled.
By August 12 it had shrunk to one unnamed line in The Leader. None of these reports questioned the mob, and no Black-press coverage was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Samuel Johnson
bases: A mob hanged Samuel Johnson from a tree over an accusation of assaulting a white woman and left him for dead; he survived, so this was an attempted lynching (A1, A3).

A mob hanged Johnson without lawful authority over an accusation of assaulting a white woman, but Black passersby cut him down and he revived, so no one was killed (A1, A3, A4); this was an attempted lynching. The mob's size is not given.

Two separately worded Macon dispatches (A1 by telegraph to the Tribune, A3 a wire) agree on the hanging, the rescue, and the discovery by health officers, and a later brief (A4) confirms the survival and jailing.

accounts.label: Macon dispatch to the New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: Johnson, 'accused of assaulting' a white woman, was hanged Tuesday night, revived by Black passersby, found by health officers and jailed, to be returned to the scene if he recovered.

accounts.label: Johnson's own story (Macon wire)
accounts.gist: According to Johnson, the mob left immediately after hanging him; a party of Black men found and cut down the body and revived him.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'LYNCHED NEGRO STILL ALIVE' with the subhead 'Mob Will Have Another Chance', while its text kept the charge as an accusation.
The Waterbury Evening Democrat ran the Macon wire under 'Lynched Negro Still Lives' and called Johnson 'the negro who attacked a white woman', stating the charge as fact.
The Leader reduced the story to a one-line item without name or place.
